explainers.title: Getting started: our welcome poem
explainers.body: A new family has moved to our town, with boxes and bags. They have come to make a new home. Look at a picture of a family arriving, or just imagine it. What can you see? How do you think they feel? Then read this poem out loud together, and join in on the last line!

explainers.title: 1. Why do families move?
explainers.body:
Families move to a new place for happy reasons. Read each one with your grown-up. Talk about it.

When a family moves, they need to find out about their new area. There is a lot to learn! Match each thing to why they need it. Draw a line, or say it out loud.

rows: so they can see a doctor if they are ill
so the children have somewhere to play
so they can buy their food

explainers.title: 2. Ask someone who moved
explainers.body:
Lots of people have moved to a new city. My grandmother, Ayeeyo, moved from Mogadishu to Hargeisa when she was a girl. She said it felt exciting, and a little bit hard at first, because she missed her friends. But soon she made new friends and grew to love her new home.

Ask a grown-up in your family who once moved, like a grandparent, aunt or uncle. Ask them these gentle questions, and tell your grown-up what they said.

explainers.title: 3. Our neighbourhood by numbers
explainers.body:
An infographic is a picture that shows facts using numbers. Here is a simple one about our growing neighbourhood, where new families come to live. Read it with your grown-up.

Talk about it: lots of children live near us, and new children arrive too. That means lots of chances to make a new friend!
bullets: Almost 1 in every ______ people who live here is a child. (Is it 3, or 10?)
About 1 in every ______ people who move here is a child your age. (Is it 3, or 10?)
Our neighbourhood is getting ______ and bigger. (bigger, or smaller?)

explainers.title: 4. Happy, healthy, safe, and belong
explainers.body: When a new child like Amina starts at our school, we want her to feel four things. Read them with your grown-up.

rows: We can play games together at break time.
There is a time to eat and drink water.
We can tell a grown-up if we feel upset.
Everyone is welcome to join in.

explainers.title: 5. Kind feelings, kind actions
explainers.body:
When we know how a feeling works, we know a kind thing to do. Match each feeling to a kind action. Draw a line, or say it out loud.

Now draw one thing a new child needs to know at our school. Then tell your grown-up about your picture. Use these words: In my picture I have shown how you can ... and This helps you to ...

rows: We feel happy when people are kind.
So we should be kind to others.
We feel safe because grown-ups look after us.
So we should tell a grown-up if something is not right.
We feel proud when we do well.
So we should try our best.
We feel we belong when we are included.
So we should help others feel welcome and join in.

headers: Draw one thing a new child needs to know

explainers.title: 6. A little survey and report
explainers.body:
Let's find out what other children think! A survey means asking lots of people the same questions. Ask a few friends or family members these three questions. Draw a happy face for each answer, or write a word.

Now tell your grown-up a little report of what you found out. You can start like this:
bullets: Children in my class are happy when they ...

rows: What makes you happy at school?

explainers.title: 7. Yusuf's letter
explainers.body: My cousin Yusuf moved far away to a new town called Nuuria, for his mum and dad's new jobs. He sent me this letter. Read it with your grown-up, and think about how Yusuf feels.

explainers.title: 8. Write a kind advice letter
explainers.body: Let's send Yusuf, and any new child, some kind advice. Advice is friendly words that help someone know what to do. Finish these kind sentences. Say them out loud, or write them.
bullets: It is a good idea to ...

explainers.title: 9. Start planning: what does a new child need?
explainers.body:
Soon your team will make a role play to welcome a new child like Amina. First, let's think of everything a new child needs. In the box, start a mind map. Write 'Welcome to our school!' in the middle, then draw lines to your ideas.

Tell your team your best idea. Listen to their ideas too. You will make the whole role play together on the next sheet!

headers: Our mind map: Welcome to our school!

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You thought about moving and welcoming today. That was so kind! Answer these out loud with your grown-up.

Well done! Now turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to make your very own welcome role play with your team.
bullets: How might a new child feel on their first day?
What is one kind thing you could do to help them?
What makes you feel like you belong?

bigIdeas.title: Our growing neighbourhood

bigIdeas.title: Four good feelings
lines: Happy — feeling glad and having fun.
Healthy — eating well, drinking water, and washing our hands.
Safe — being looked after by kind grown-ups.
Belong — feeling like you are part of the group.
Read each thing our school does. Match it to the feeling it gives. Draw a line, or say it out loud.

bigIdeas.title: A letter from Yusuf
lines: Dear Ayaan,
We have lived in Nuuria for three months now. Mum and Dad are happy with their new jobs.
Everything here is new. We live in a new home, and the food is different. I am trying it, and some of it is nice!
I am learning the new words. I can say hello, please and thank you.
My new school is not open yet, so I have not made many friends. It is a little hard.
I miss my old friends, and I miss playing our favourite game. But I am trying my best.
Please write back soon!
From your cousin, Yusuf

How do you think Yusuf feels? He feels happy about some things and sad about some things. That is called feeling a bit of both, and it is completely okay. Tell your grown-up one thing that makes Yusuf happy, and one thing that is hard for him.

bigIdeas.title: Kind advice for a new child
lines: Make friends by joining in a game.
Learn new words by talking to people and trying the words you know.
Smile, and say hello.
Listen carefully to your new friends.
Soon your school will open, and you will meet lots of new children.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.
notes: please read every part aloud. Your child can point, talk, draw, act, tick and match. There are no marks. Just have fun together, and keep it warm and kind.

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to your child's next Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up who will run the unit with your child. Six- and seven-year-olds are early readers, so you will read most of it aloud, look at the pictures together, and do lots of talking, drawing and acting. Underneath all that fun, your child is quietly growing big thinking-and-doing skills: understanding how it feels to move somewhere new, finding things out, using numbers, imagining how other people feel, sharing kind ideas, working with others, and looking back at their learning.

This project grows those skills through a warm and gentle topic: moving to a new place, and how we welcome a newcomer. Imagine a new family has just moved to your neighbourhood, and a new child is starting at your child's school. How would they feel? What would help them? How can we be kind and help them feel at home? Welcoming a guest warmly is one of the most beautiful parts of who we are, so your child already has a big, kind heart for this.

You do not need to be a teacher, and you do not need anything special. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, some paper and crayons, and a willingness to let your child talk, look, draw and act. That is exactly how these skills grow. Keep the whole unit warm and hopeful. Moving is an adventure, and a new child is a new friend.

sections.title: About this project: What is it like to move here?
sections.body:
Over this unit, you and your child will explore one big, gentle question: what is it like to move to a new place? Your child will think about why families move, what a new family needs to find out about an area, and how a newcomer might feel. They will find out what helps children feel happy, healthy and safe and feel that they belong. They will read a kind letter from a child who has moved far away, write some friendly advice, and, best of all, work with a team to make a role play that shows how we welcome a new child to our school.

The journey is broken into six short, picture-led lessons (4.1 to 4.6), then the group role play, then a gentle looking-back. The topic is the warm, human part; the real learning is happening quietly underneath it.

sections.title: What your child will gently grow
sections.body:
This project grows several Global Perspectives skills, all woven quietly into the topic. Here they are in plain words, with what to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give any marks. You simply give your child lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A warm 'That was so kind, Ayaan' teaches more than any worksheet ever could.
items: Understanding the issue — seeing what it is like to move, and what helps a newcomer belong. Listen for: 'They might feel a bit shy.' and 'We could help them.'
Finding out (a little research) — asking a relative who moved, and asking other children what they think. Listen for: 'Let's ask.' and 'What do you think helps?'
Using numbers (a little analysis) — reading a simple infographic and finishing number sentences. Listen for: 'Almost one in three is a child!'
Imagining how others feel (empathy) — picturing how a new child feels, happy and shy at the same time. Listen for: 'I would feel ...'
Sharing kind ideas (communication) — giving friendly advice and telling others in a role play. Listen for: 'You could try ...' and 'Welcome!'
Working together (collaboration) — sharing the parts in the role play, taking turns, and helping the team.
Thinking about our learning (reflection) — looking back at what was easy, what was harder, and what helped.

sections.title: The learning goals, in child-friendly words
sections.body: Here are the little goals for this unit. They are written the way we say them to children. There are no codes to remember.
items: I can talk about what it is like to move to a new place.
I can use numbers to say what I have found out.
I can find out what other children think about our school.
I can imagine how it would feel to move somewhere new.
I can think of helpful things to tell a child who is new.
I can help my group make a role play to welcome a new child.
I can tell others about our school, and ask and answer questions.
I can talk about what I learned, and what helped me.

sections.title: A gentle note: talking about moving with care
sections.body: Moving home is a big thing in a child's world, and some children in your family or class may have moved themselves, or have loved ones who have moved to another city or country. So we keep this topic warm, gentle and positive the whole way through. Please hold these few things in mind:
items: Keep the reasons happy. In this unit, families move for good reasons: a new job, a new home, or to be near family. We do not talk about sad or scary reasons for moving. Keep every example hopeful.
Follow your child's lead, kindly. If your child mentions something sad from real life, listen with love, keep your words gentle, and softly bring the talk back to how we welcome and help a newcomer.
Every family's story is welcome. Some children will have moved and some will not. Let each child share only if they want to. There is no right story and no wrong story.
Build on our kindness. Welcoming a guest warmly, our hospitality, is a strong and beautiful part of our culture. This unit simply turns that same kindness towards a new neighbour and a new classmate.

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age are still early readers, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's young model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no fixed timetable. Spread the six lessons across two or three weeks, or longer. If your child wants to act out the welcome five times, wonderful. Kindness and curiosity are the whole point.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read the lessons and the welcome poem aloud, run the simple activities, and keep everything warm and playful. Each lesson is short, about 20 to 35 minutes, and you can split it into smaller pieces or stop when your child has had enough.

Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these live sessions children look at pictures together, share their ideas, do the survey, and perform their role plays for other learners. The role play works best with a small group.

A 24-hour AI tutor, always used with a grown-up. The AI tutor can read a lesson aloud, ask your child a friendly question, help look something up, or be a kind pretend audience while your child rehearses the role play. At this age the tutor is always used with you sitting right beside your child, never on their own.

sections.title: Meet Ayaan and his friends
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a boy called Ayaan. He goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa, and he has a kind heart and lots of ideas. Your child can imagine working right alongside him and his friends.

This unit has three more gentle characters your child will meet:

Together, Ayaan and his friends are a little welcome team. As your child meets each new idea, they will see what Ayaan's team does with it. Later, your child will do the very same thing with their own team, which can be classmates, brothers and sisters, or friends.
items: Ayaan loves to help people. When someone is new, he wants them to feel at home.
Hodan is thoughtful and asks good questions. She likes to find out how people feel.
Bilal knows his way around and loves to show people where things are.
Sagal is kind and careful, and good at remembering the plan.
Layla is cheerful and friendly, and always ready to say hello.
Omar likes to share the jobs fairly so everyone has a turn.

Amina is a girl who has just moved to Ayaan's neighbourhood with her family, for her mother's new job. She is starting at Ehel Academy. She feels excited, and a little shy. The role play is all about helping Amina feel welcome.
Yusuf is Ayaan's cousin. His family moved far away to a new town called Nuuria, for their new jobs. Yusuf writes a kind letter about what it is like to be the new one.
Ayeeyo is Ayaan's grandmother. When she was a girl, she moved from Mogadishu to Hargeisa. She has a lovely story to share about it.

sections.title: How to read the arriving-family picture and the welcome poem aloud
sections.body:
This unit opens with a happy picture: a new family arriving in the neighbourhood with their boxes and bags, ready to make a new home. If you have a picture like this, look at it together. If not, simply imagine it. Then talk about it gently, using questions like these:

Next, read this little welcome poem aloud. Read it slowly, twice. Run your finger under the words. The second time, let your child join in, especially the last line.
items: Who can you see? What are they carrying? Where do you think they have come to live?
How do you think the family feels? (Excited, tired, a little unsure, and hopeful.)
What will they need to find out about our area? (Where is the school? Where is the clinic? Where can the children play? Where is the market?)
How can we help them feel welcome on their very first day?

sections.title: How to run the six short lessons
sections.body: Each lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for, just for you), a Talk about part (to get your child thinking and speaking), and a Do part (the hands-on activity). Read the Aim to yourself, then enjoy the Talk about and Do parts with your child. Lots of talking is exactly right. Keep everything short and cheerful.

sections.title: Lesson 4.1 - What does it mean to move to a new place?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child learns that families move for happy reasons, and that a new family needs to find out about their new area. Your child also meets a simple infographic and uses numbers. New words: move, area, information, infographic.

Talk about. Look at the arriving-family picture together. Ask: 'How do you think this family feels? What will they need to find out about where we live?' Every kind guess is welcome.

Do. First, talk gently about why families move. Keep it happy: for a new job, for a new home, or to be near family. Then talk about the information a new family needs to find out. There are lots of important things:

sections.title: Lesson 4.2 - What do we need when we start at a new school?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child thinks about what helps children feel happy, healthy and safe and feel that they belong, and finds out what other children think. New words: belong, happy, healthy, safe.

Talk about. Amina is new at our school. Ask: 'What are the important things Amina needs to know? What would help her feel happy here?' Let your child think of the things they know about school that a new child might not.

Do. Talk about the kind things at school that help children feel happy, healthy, safe, and that they belong. For example: you can talk to an adult if you feel upset; we are careful crossing the road; there is a time to eat and drink; there is a time to play and sing. Then play the kind feelings, kind actions game: draw a line from each feeling to a kind action.

Then let your child draw one thing a new child needs to know, and tell you about it using 'In my picture I have shown how you can ...' and 'This helps you to ...'. Finish with a little survey: your child asks a few classmates or family members 'What makes you happy at school? What helps you stay healthy? What helps you feel safe?' and then tells you a short report of what they found, like 'Children in my class are happy when they play together.'
items: We feel happy when people are kind — so we should be kind to others.
We feel safe because adults look after us — so we should tell an adult if something is not right.
We feel proud when we do well — so we should try our best.
We feel like we belong when we are included — so we should help others feel welcome and join in.

sections.title: Lesson 4.3 - What would it feel like to move somewhere new?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child imagines how it feels to move somewhere new, by reading a kind letter from a child who has moved. This is the gentle, caring heart of the unit. New word: advice.

Talk about. Ask softly: 'How do you think you would feel if you moved somewhere new and far away? Excited? A little shy? Both at once?' All feelings are okay.

Do. Read Yusuf's letter together (it is on the Activity Sheet). Yusuf is Ayaan's cousin. His family moved to a faraway town called Nuuria for their new jobs, three months ago. Yusuf writes that his mum and dad are happy in their new work, everything is new, the food is different and he is trying it, and he is learning some new words to say hello and thank you. But his new school is not open yet, it is hard to make friends, and he misses his old friends. Ask your child: 'How does Yusuf feel? Happy, sad, or a bit of both?' The gentle answer is a bit of both, and that is completely normal.

Then help your child write a friendly advice letter to a new child, thinking about how they feel and what words would help. Kind advice might be: make friends by joining in games; learn new words by talking to people and trying the words you know; smile; listen carefully; and soon you will meet lots of new children. Useful sentence starters are 'You could try asking ...', 'It is a good idea to ...', 'It is important to ...' and 'Why don't you ...'. Praise every kind idea warmly.

sections.title: Lesson 4.4 - How can we help new children? Let's plan a role play.
sections.body:
Aim. Your child helps a team plan a role play about welcoming a new child, showing how we help them feel happy, healthy and safe. This is where the big project begins. New words: role play, mind map.

Talk about. Explain what a role play is: we pretend to be other people to show something. Ask: 'If you could act out one kind thing to help Amina, what would it be?'

Do. First, make a mind map called 'Welcome to our school!'. Write that in the middle, then draw branches for what a new child needs: to be healthy (bring a water bottle, where to eat, wash your hands), to do well (borrow a library book, ask for help, join in), to be happy (make friends, play games, kind words), and to feel safe (who to ask, walk do not run, tell a grown-up). Then help the group plan the role play in a table: decide what you will say and who will say it. Agree a few simple teamwork rules, such as 'speak clearly so everyone can hear'. The full steps are in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet.

sections.title: Lesson 4.5 - How can we perform and talk about our role play?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child performs the role play, tells other children about the school, and asks and answers friendly questions. New word: improve.

Talk about. Ask: 'What is the very first thing you will say to welcome the new child? How will you make your voice warm and friendly?'

Do. First rehearse at home with you, and with the AI tutor as a kind pretend audience. Then perform the role play for real, for the family or for other children in the twice-weekly teacher session. After the first go, help the group improve it: listen back, and use the top tips (Did you give helpful tips? Did you show how to enjoy the new school? Did you speak clearly? Did everyone get a turn?). Use kind words like 'I like the way ...' and 'I think we should ...', then perform it again, even better. Finally, visit other groups' role plays: ask a relevant question and then a follow-up question, and answer the questions people ask about yours. Afterwards, talk about the best ideas you heard, using 'I really liked the way they ...' and 'That is a good idea for new children because ...'.

sections.title: Lesson 4.6 - What have we learned?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child looks back at the whole project: what they now know about moving and welcoming, what they can do, the good ideas others had, and what helped them learn. This is the reflection, and it matters as much as the role play.

Talk about. Ask gently: 'What do you know now about moving to a new place? How can we help someone who is new? What was easy? What was harder?'

Do. The full reflection, with faces to point to, stars to colour, and warm talking questions, is in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Do it warmly and out loud. Celebrate the kindness and the thinking, not just the role play.

sections.title: Gentle discussion prompts
sections.body: Talking is where most of the learning happens at this age. Sprinkle these warm questions through your days together. There are no right answers, only kind thinking.
items: How do you think a new child feels on their very first day?
What is one kind thing we could do to help them feel welcome?
Can you remember a time you were new somewhere? How did it feel?
What makes you feel happy and safe at school?
What does it mean to belong? When do you feel you belong?
If a new family moved next door, what could our family do to help?
Why is it good to welcome a guest warmly?

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the words your child will meet in this project. Say them often and warmly. There is no need to test them.

rows: To go and live in a new place.
The part of a town where you live. We also call it our neighbourhood.
A person who has just moved to a new place.
To be kind and happy when someone new comes.
The things we need to know, like where the school is.
A picture that shows facts using numbers.
Something important that people think about together.
To plan how something will look before you make it.
One thing that shows what you mean.
To feel you are part of a group, and that you are welcome.
Feeling well and strong, with good food, water and clean hands.
Looked after by kind grown-ups, so you feel calm and cared for.
Kind words that help someone know what to do.
Asking lots of people the same question to find something out.
Pretending to be other people to show something.
A picture that puts all our ideas around one big idea.
Being warm and helpful to other people.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy at all. Gather a few of these before you start, and keep them in a box:
items: Paper and crayons or coloured pencils.
One big sheet of paper for the group's mind map.
A picture of a family arriving somewhere new, if you have one (or just imagine it together).
A few simple props for the role play, like a bag or a hat (optional, and fun).
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.
A warm voice and a little time, about twice a week.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient, friendly helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in your child's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep it short and cheerful, and always stay right there. If the tutor ever suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it. You are always in charge.
items: Read aloud. Ask it to read a lesson, the welcome poem, or Yusuf's letter slowly, so your child can follow.
Ask a friendly question. Ask it to ask your child one question about welcoming a newcomer, then let your child answer out loud to you.
Help look something up. Ask it a gentle question together, such as 'How do you say hello in another language?', and enjoy the answer.
Rehearse the role play. Let the tutor be a kind pretend audience while your child practises the welcome, before performing for family or the class.

sections.title: The final task: a role play about welcoming a new child
sections.body:
Everything leads gently to this. In a team of a few children, your child will make a role play that shows how we welcome a new child to our school and help them feel happy, healthy and safe. The team makes a mind map of what a new child needs, decides what to say and who will say it, agrees a few teamwork rules, rehearses, and then performs the role play and answers questions about it.

The full, child-friendly steps and the group plan are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Your job is to gather the paper and props, keep the team kind and fair so everyone has a part, and help only when they are truly stuck. A warm, wobbly, hand-made role play that your child is proud of is exactly what success looks like at this age.

sections.title: Simple ways to support and extend
sections.body:
Every child is different. Here are gentle ways to make the unit easier, or to add a little more for a child who is ready.

To support a child who finds it tricky:

To extend a child who wants more:
items: Read every part aloud, and let your child point, draw or act instead of writing.
Do one small piece at a time, and stop while it is still fun.
Act out the welcome with toys or puppets first, before real people.
Let your child say their advice out loud instead of writing it. Talking always counts.
Learn how to say 'hello' and 'welcome' in one more language, and use it together.
Draw a little map of the neighbourhood to show a new family where things are.
Add more parts to the role play, like showing the new child the library or the market.
Let your child teach you one kind thing they learned. Teaching is the best way to remember.

sections.title: Thinking about our learning: a simple reflection
sections.body:
To finish, help your child look back and feel good about what they did and thought. Keep it gentle and spoken. The Mini-Project & Reflection sheet has happy faces to point to, stars to colour, and warm questions such as:

This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill (reflection), and it matters as much as the role play. When children hear that their kindness and their thinking are valued, they learn a lesson that lasts far longer than any fact.
items: What is one thing you know now about moving to a new place?
How can you help a child who is new feel welcome?
What good idea did someone else in your team have?
What was easy? What was harder?
How did you help your team? How did they help you?

sections.title: Keeping it warm and kind
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, keep the mood cheerful, and talk far more than you worry about getting it 'right'. Remember the golden rule of this unit: always warm, always kind, always hopeful. If your child finishes believing that moving is an adventure, and that they can help a new friend feel happy, safe and welcome, then this project has done its job beautifully. Have fun, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is the big one! At Ehel Academy, Ayaan and his friends made a role play to welcome a new child, and now it is your turn. With your team and a grown-up, you are going to plan and act out a role play that shows how we welcome a new child and help them feel happy, healthy and safe. Then you will look back at how your team did. Take your time, share the parts, and be kind to each other.

steps.title: Make a mind map of what a new child needs
steps.intro: A mind map puts all our ideas around one big idea. Write 'Welcome to our school!' in the middle of the box. Then draw lines to your ideas. Use these four branches to help you.

headers: Our mind map: Welcome to our school!

steps.title: Choose your parts
steps.intro:
Everyone needs a part to play. Decide together who will be who. If lots of you want the same part, take turns or have a quick vote.

Write your team's names next to the parts.

rows: Pretends to be new, like Amina, and says hello.
Says a warm hello and shows the new child around.
Shows where to eat, drink and wash hands.
Asks the new child to join in a game.

steps.title: Plan what to say and who says it
steps.intro:
Now plan your role play. Decide what you will say, and who will say it. Here is how Ayaan's team planned theirs, to help you.

Now make your own plan. Write what each person will say. Keep it short and warm.

rows: Hello! Welcome to our school. My name is Ayaan.
We will show you around and help you feel at home.
Here is our classroom, and here is where we play.
Here is where we have our water and wash our hands.
If you feel worried, you can ask me or our teacher.
Come and play with us! You can join our game.

steps.title: Agree your teamwork rules
steps.intro: A good role play needs a few kind rules, so it works well for everyone. Here are two to start. Talk about them, then think of two more of your own.
items: Speak clearly, so everyone can hear.
Everyone gets a turn to speak.

steps.title: Practise with your team
steps.intro: Now practise your role play together. Stand up and act it out. Say your words in a warm, friendly voice. It is fine if you forget a bit, or giggle. That happens to real actors too! Just try again.

steps.title: Perform your role play
steps.intro: When you have practised, perform your role play for real! Show it to your family, or to other children in your teacher session. Speak clearly and warmly. Remember, your role play shows how a new child will feel happy, healthy, safe, and that they belong.

steps.title: Make it even better
steps.intro:
After your first go, talk about how to make it better. This is called making it improve. Read each top tip and point to a happy face if you did it, or a straight face if it is not quite there yet.

Now say one kind thing and one better thing. Use these words: I like the way ... and I think we should ... Then perform your role play again, even better!

rows: We gave the new child helpful tips.
We showed how to enjoy our school.

steps.title: Ask and answer questions
steps.intro:
Now visit another team's role play. Watch it, then ask a relevant question, one that is really about their welcome. After they answer, ask a follow-up question to find out a little more. Then answer the questions people ask about your role play, kindly.

Here are some question starters to help you:

Afterwards, talk about the best ideas you saw in other role plays. Finish these out loud:
items: Why did you show the new child ...?
What would help the new child feel ...?
And then what happened next?
I really liked the way they ...
It was interesting to hear about ...
That is a good idea for new children because ...

steps.title: Good ideas others had
steps.intro: Our friends have good ideas too. Finish these two sentences out loud.
items: A good idea my friend had was ...
I would like to try their idea of ...

steps.title: What helped me learn
steps.intro:
We did lots of things in this project. Tick the ones you liked best. Then say how each one helped you learn.

Now finish these out loud. Use words like This helped me to ...
items: ☐ Looking at the infographic with numbers.
☐ Making a mind map.
☐ Finding out what other children think.
☐ Doing the welcome role play.
I looked at the infographic. This helped me to ...
I made a mind map. This helped me to ...
I found out other children's ideas. This helped me to ...
I did the role play. This helped me to ...

steps.title: How we have been good learners
steps.intro:
A good learner does kind and clever things. Read these, and tick the ones you did. Then tell your grown-up about one of them.

Finish this sentence out loud: I have been a good learner because I ...

Well done! You imagined how a newcomer feels, you shared kind ideas, you worked as a team, and you showed how to make a new child feel welcome. That is exactly what a good, kind Global Perspectives thinker does. A new child is a new friend, and now you know just how to help!
items: ☐ I thought about other people's ideas carefully.
☐ I came up with a new idea of my own.
☐ I kept working and never gave up.
☐ I remembered what my team needed.

reflection.prompt: I now know that moving to a new place can feel ...
When someone is new, I can help by ...
A new child feels they belong when ...

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: Our role play shows how to welcome a new child.
We thought about how a new child feels.
Everyone had a part and said their bit.
We took turns and listened to each other.
